summary.text: Finite initial checks seed a self-similarity induction for the run-length hierarchy, yielding eventual recurrences for the row sum \(a_n\), row length \(L_n\), number of runs \(r_n\), and the next run-count \(q_n\): \(a_{n+1}=a_n+L_n\), \(L_{n+1}=L_n+r_n\), \(r_{n+1}=r_n+q_n-1\), and \(q_{n+1}=q_n+L_{n-4}\). For a root \(\lambda\in(3/2,2)\) of \(\lambda^4(\lambda-1)^3=1\), a positive weighted potential in \(L,r,q\) and four lagged lengths satisfies an exact affine geometric recurrence and is comparable to \(L_n\); hence \(L_n\), and then \(a_n\), lie between positive constant multiples of \(\lambda^n\), so taking \(n\)-th roots gives the limit \(\lambda\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(R(X)\) denote the run-length encoding of a finite list \(X\): each maximal block of equal consecutive entries is replaced by the length of that block. We write juxtaposition for concatenation, \(\operatorname{rev}X\) for reversal, \(X^-\) for the list obtained by deleting the last entry, and \(\operatorname{tail}X\) for the list obtained by deleting the first entry.

Define the rows \(T_n\) by
\[
T_1=[1],\qquad T_2=[1],\qquad T_3=[2],
\]
and, for \(n\geq 3\),
\[
T_{n+1}=R(\operatorname{rev}T_n)\,T_n.
\]
The sequence in question is
\[
a_n=\sum_{x\in T_n}x.
\]
We prove that \(a_n^{1/n}\) has a limit. In fact, the proof identifies that limit as a real number \(\lambda\in(3/2,2)\) satisfying
\[
\lambda^4(\lambda-1)^3=1.
\]

## 1. Elementary facts about run-length encoding

We first record the list facts that will be used. All of them follow directly by considering maximal constant blocks.

1. The entries of \(R(X)\) sum to the length of \(X\):
\[
\sum R(X)=|X|.
\]
Indeed, the runs partition the entries of \(X\).

2. Reversal reverses the sequence of runs but does not change their lengths:
\[
R(\operatorname{rev}X)=\operatorname{rev}(R(X)).
\]
In particular, the number of runs is invariant under reversal.

3. If \(A,B\) are nonempty, then the run encodings of \(A\) and \(B\) concatenate unless the last entry of \(A\) equals the first entry of \(B\). In the latter case, the last run of \(A\) and the first run of \(B\) merge. Thus, writing \(p\) for the last entry of \(R(A)\) and \(q\) for the first entry of \(R(B)\),
\[
R(AB)=
\begin{cases}
R(A)R(B),&\text{if the boundary entries differ},\\
R(A)^-\,[p+q] \,\operatorname{tail}(R(B)),&\text{if they agree}.
\end{cases}
\]

4. If a nonempty list \(B\) is appended to an arbitrary prefix \(A\), then \(R(AB)\) ends in \(\operatorname{tail}(R(B))\). The only run of \(B\) that can be affected by the boundary with \(A\) is its first run.

5. If the first two entries of a list are unequal, deleting the first entry simply deletes the first run length from its run encoding. If the first two entries are equal, deleting the first entry decreases the first run length by one and leaves all later run lengths unchanged.

6. If the last entry of a list is a singleton run, replacing it by another value which is also different from the preceding entry leaves its run-length encoding unchanged.

We shall also use the number of runs, denoted \(\rho(X)=|R(X)|\). Clearly
\[
\rho(X)\leq |X|,
\]
since every run contains at least one entry.

Set
\[
S_n=R(T_n),\qquad Q_n=R(S_n),\qquad U_n=R(Q_n).
\]
Using the reversal identity, the row recurrence becomes
\[
T_{n+1}=\operatorname{rev}(S_n)\,T_n. \tag{1}
\]

## 2. Structural identities for the first three transforms

Suppose that \(S_n,T_n\) are nonempty and have the same first entry. Applying the merging formula at the boundary in (1) gives
\[
S_{n+1}
 =\operatorname{rev}(\operatorname{tail}Q_n)\,
 [\operatorname{head}Q_n+\operatorname{head}S_n] \,
 \operatorname{tail}S_n. \tag{2}
\]
To see this, note that
\(R(\operatorname{rev}S_n)=\operatorname{rev}Q_n\). The last entry of \(\operatorname{rev}S_n\) is the first entry of \(S_n\), which by assumption is also the first entry of \(T_n\), so the boundary runs merge. The last run length of \(\operatorname{rev}S_n\) is the first entry of \(Q_n\), while the first run length of \(T_n\) is the first entry of \(S_n\).

Under the more specific boundary conditions
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{the first two entries of }S_n\text{ are }1,1,\\
&\operatorname{head}Q_n\geq 3,\qquad
  \text{the second entry of }Q_n\text{ is }1,
\end{aligned} \tag{3}
\]
and assuming the relevant lists have at least two entries, taking run lengths in (2) gives
\[
Q_{n+1}
 =\operatorname{rev}(\operatorname{tail}U_n)\,[1,\operatorname{head}Q_n-1] \,
 \operatorname{tail}Q_n. \tag{4}
\]
Here is the boundary analysis behind (4). The last entry of
\(\operatorname{rev}(\operatorname{tail}Q_n)\) is the second entry of \(Q_n\), namely \(1\), whereas the next entry in (2) is
\(\operatorname{head}Q_n+1\geq4\), so there is no merger there. That middle entry is itself a singleton run, contributing the displayed \(1\). Since the first two entries of \(S_n\) are both \(1\), deleting the first entry of \(S_n\) shortens the first run of \(S_n\) by one. Its run encoding is therefore
\([
\operatorname{head}Q_n-1] \,\operatorname{tail}Q_n\), giving (4).

There is one further self-similarity. Assume in addition that the first two entries of \(U_n\) are \(1,3\), and that
\[
R(U_n)=S_{n-4}. \tag{5}
\]
Taking run lengths in (4) then yields
\[
U_{n+1}
 =\operatorname{rev}(\operatorname{tail}S_{n-4})\,[1] \,U_n. \tag{6}
\]
Indeed, the reversed prefix in (4) contributes
\(\operatorname{rev}(\operatorname{tail}R(U_n))
=\operatorname{rev}(\operatorname{tail}S_{n-4})\).
Its last entry is the second entry of \(U_n\), namely \(3\), so it does not merge with the following \(1\). Also \(\operatorname{head}Q_n-1\geq2\), so this \(1\) is a singleton. Finally, changing the first entry of
\([\operatorname{head}Q_n-1]\operatorname{tail}Q_n\)
back to \(\operatorname{head}Q_n\) does not alter its run encoding, because both values are different from the second entry of \(Q_n\), which is \(1\). Its run encoding is consequently \(U_n\), proving (6).

The key word identity is
\[
U_n=T_{n-4}^-\,[6]. \tag{7}
\]
It implies (5), provided the last two entries of \(T_{n-4}\) are \(1,2\). In fact, replacing the final \(2\) of \(T_{n-4}\) by \(6\) leaves the run encoding unchanged, since in either case the final value differs from the preceding \(1\). Thus
\[
R(U_n)=R(T_{n-4}^- [6])=R(T_{n-4})=S_{n-4}.
\]
Moreover, (7) propagates. Assuming (6), (7), and that \(S_{n-4}\) starts with \(1\), we have
\[
\operatorname{rev}S_{n-4}
 =\operatorname{rev}(\operatorname{tail}S_{n-4})[1].
\]
Using (1), with index \(n-4\), and then deleting the last entry, gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
T_{n+1-4}^-[6]
 &=T_{(n-4)+1}^-[6]\\
 &=\bigl(\operatorname{rev}S_{n-4}\,T_{n-4}\bigr)^-[6]\\
 &=\operatorname{rev}(\operatorname{tail}S_{n-4})[1]T_{n-4}^-[6]\\
 &=\operatorname{rev}(\operatorname{tail}S_{n-4})[1]U_n\\
 &=U_{n+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
So (7) at \(n\) implies (7) at \(n+1\), once the stated boundary facts are known.

## 3. The invariant and its induction

We now state all boundary information needed to justify the preceding identities uniformly. For every \(n\geq10\), we claim:

\[
\begin{array}{ll}
\text{(i)}&T_n\text{ begins with }1,3,\text{ ends with }1,2,\text{ and }|T_n|\geq4;\\
\text{(ii)}&S_n\text{ begins with }1,1,\text{ ends with }3,1,\text{ and }|S_n|\geq4;\\
\text{(iii)}&\operatorname{head}Q_n\geq3,
   \ Q_n\text{ has second entry }1,
   \ Q_n\text{ ends with }1,1,
   \text{ and }|Q_n|\geq4;\\
\text{(iv)}&U_n=T_{n-4}^-[6].
\end{array} \tag{8}
\]

We also need a weaker statement for every \(m\geq6\):
\[
T_m\text{ begins with }1,3,\text{ ends with }1,2,\ |T_m|\geq4,
\quad S_m\text{ begins with }1. \tag{9}
\]

The finite starting calculation is as follows. Successively applying the row recurrence gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
T_6&=[1,3,1,1,1,2],\\
T_7&=[1,3,1,1,1,3,1,1,1,2],\\
T_8&=[1,3,1,3,1,1,1,3,1,1,1,3,1,1,1,2],\\
T_9&=[1,3,1,3,1,3,1,1,1,1,1,3,1,3,1,1,1,3,1,1,1,3,1,1,1,2],\\
T_{10}&=[1,3,1,3,1,3,1,1,1,5,1,1,1,1,1,1,1,3,1,3,1,3,1,1,1,1,\\
&\hspace{22mm}1,3,1,3,1,1,1,3,1,1,1,3,1,1,1,2].
\end{aligned}
\]
Directly grouping equal adjacent entries shows that (9) holds for \(m=6,7,8,9\). For the full base case,
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_{10}&=[1,1,1,1,1,1,3,1,7,1,1,1,1,1,5,1,1,1,3,1,3,1,3,1],\\
Q_{10}&=[6,1,1,1,5,1,3,1,1,1,1,1,1],\\
U_{10}&=[1,3,1,1,1,6]=T_6^-[6].
\end{aligned}
\]
These lists establish every part of (8) at \(n=10\).

We next prove the inductive step. Assume (8) at \(n\), and assume (9) at \(n-4\). Identity (7) and (9) show that \(U_n\) begins with \(1,3\), ends with \(1,6\), has length at least four, and satisfies (5). Hence (2), (4), and (6) all apply, and the propagation argument above proves (7) for \(n+1\).

It remains to check the boundary and length clauses of (8) at \(n+1\). These checks explain why all clauses were included.

From (1), the first two entries of \(T_{n+1}\) are the last and penultimate entries of \(S_n\), hence \(1,3\). Its last two entries are inherited from the suffix \(T_n\), hence are \(1,2\).

From (2), its reversed initial block shows that the first two entries of \(S_{n+1}\) are the last and penultimate entries of \(Q_n\), hence \(1,1\). The general suffix property of run encoding says that \(S_{n+1}\) ends with \(\operatorname{tail}S_n\); therefore its final two entries remain \(3,1\).

From (4), the first two entries of \(Q_{n+1}\) are the last and penultimate entries of \(U_n\), namely \(6,1\). In particular its first entry is at least \(3\). Again its suffix is \(\operatorname{tail}Q_n\), so its final two entries remain \(1,1\).

The length bounds also persist. More precisely, taking lengths in (1), (2), and (4) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
|T_{n+1}|&=|T_n|+|S_n|, \tag{10}\\
|S_{n+1}|&=|S_n|+|Q_n|-1, \tag{11}\\
|Q_{n+1}|&=|Q_n|+|U_n|. \tag{12}
\end{aligned}
\]
All quantities on the right have the required positive lower bounds, so the three lengths remain at least four. This completes the inductive step.

A strong induction now proves (8) for all \(n\geq10\). Indeed, the base is \(n=10\). To obtain the assertion at \(n+1\), the induction hypothesis supplies (8) at \(n\). The needed weaker assertion (9) at \(n-4\) is one of the finite cases \(6,7,8,9\) if \(n-4<10\), and otherwise follows immediately from (8) at \(n-4\). The same argument also proves (9) for every \(m\geq6\).

A useful consequence of (7) is
\[
|U_n|=|T_{n-4}|\qquad(n\geq10), \tag{13}
\]
because deleting the last entry and appending \(6\) does not change the length.

## 4. Recurrences for the relevant numerical sequences

Define
\[
L_n=|T_n|,\qquad r_n=|S_n|,\qquad q_n=|Q_n|.
\]
Equation (10) gives, for \(n\geq3\),
\[
L_{n+1}=L_n+r_n. \tag{14}
\]
Equation (11), justified by the invariant, gives for \(n\geq10\),
\[
r_{n+1}=r_n+q_n-1. \tag{15}
\]
Equations (12) and (13) give for \(n\geq10\),
\[
q_{n+1}=q_n+L_{n-4}. \tag{16}
\]
Finally, the newly prepended part in the definition of \(T_{n+1}\) is a run-length encoding of \(\operatorname{rev}T_n\), whose entries sum to \(|T_n|\). Therefore
\[
a_{n+1}=a_n+L_n \qquad(n\geq3). \tag{17}
\]

We will also need simple inequalities. The sequence \(L_n\) is nondecreasing: this is immediate from (14) for \(n\geq3\), and the finitely many earlier cases are direct. Since a run encoding has no more entries than its input,
\[
0\leq q_n\leq r_n\leq L_n. \tag{18}
\]
Also the displayed value of \(T_{10}\) gives
\[
L_{10}=42\geq4,
\qquad a_{10}>0. \tag{19}
\]

## 5. A geometric potential

Let
\[
f(x)=x^4(x-1)^3.
\]
This is continuous. Moreover
\[
f(3/2)=\frac{81}{128}<1,
\qquad f(2)=16>1.
\]
Thus the intermediate value theorem supplies some
\(\lambda\in(3/2,2)\) such that
\[
\lambda^4(\lambda-1)^3=1. \tag{20}
\]
In particular, \(\lambda>1\).

For \(n\geq10\), define the potential
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Phi_n={}&L_n+\frac{r_n}{\lambda-1}
 +\frac{q_n}{(\lambda-1)^2}
 +(\lambda-1)L_{n-1}
 +\lambda(\lambda-1)L_{n-2}\\
&+\lambda^2(\lambda-1)L_{n-3}
 +\lambda^3(\lambda-1)L_{n-4}.
\end{aligned} \tag{21}
\]
Substituting (14)--(16) into \(\Phi_{n+1}\), shifting the four delayed \(L\)-terms, and using (20), gives
\[
\Phi_{n+1}=\lambda\Phi_n-\frac1{\lambda-1}. \tag{22}
\]
For completeness, the cancellation can be seen by comparing coefficients. The coefficients of \(r_n\) and \(q_n\) become respectively
\(1+1/(\lambda-1)=\lambda/(\lambda-1)\) and
\(1/(\lambda-1)+1/(\lambda-1)^2=\lambda/(\lambda-1)^2\), as required for \(\lambda\Phi_n\). The shifted coefficients of \(L_n,L_{n-1},L_{n-2},L_{n-3}\) likewise match. The remaining coefficient of \(L_{n-4}\) matches precisely because
\(1/(\lambda-1)^2=\lambda^4(\lambda-1)\), which is equivalent to (20). The \(-1\) in (15) contributes the constant
\(-1/(\lambda-1)\).

The fixed point of the affine recurrence (22) is
\[
C=\frac1{(\lambda-1)^2}.
\]
Consequently, for every \(n\geq10\),
\[
\Phi_n-C=\lambda^{n-10}(\Phi_{10}-C). \tag{23}
\]
Because \(\lambda>3/2\), we have \(C<4\). Every term in (21) is nonnegative and the first is \(L_n\), so
\[
\Phi_{10}\geq L_{10}\geq4>C.
\]
Set
\[
K=\Phi_{10}-C>0.
\]
Then (23) reads
\[
\Phi_n=C+K\lambda^{n-10}. \tag{24}
\]

We compare \(\Phi_n\) with \(L_n\). Positivity of all coefficients in (21) gives
\[
L_n\leq\Phi_n. \tag{25}
\]
On the other hand, by monotonicity of \(L_n\), by (18), and because all coefficients are positive,
\[
\Phi_n\leq D L_n, \tag{26}
\]
where the positive constant
\[
D=1+\frac1{\lambda-1}+\frac1{(\lambda-1)^2}
 +(\lambda-1)+\lambda(\lambda-1)
 +\lambda^2(\lambda-1)+\lambda^3(\lambda-1)

depends only on \(\lambda\). Indeed, in (21) replace \(r_n,q_n,L_{n-j}\) by the upper bound \(L_n\).

Equations (24)--(26) give two-sided geometric bounds for \(L_n\). For an upper bound, since \(\lambda^{n-10}\geq1\) and \(\lambda^{n-10}\leq\lambda^n\),
\[
L_n\leq C+K\lambda^{n-10}
 \leq(C+K)\lambda^n.

talking
\]
(The isolated word “talking” in the preceding display is to be disregarded; the mathematical statement is the displayed inequality.)
For the lower bound, (24) and (26) imply
\[
K\lambda^{n-10}\leq D L_n.
\]
Thus, with
\[
c_L=\frac{K}{D\lambda^{10}}>0,
\qquad C_L=C+K>0,
\]
we have, for all \(n\geq10\),
\[
c_L\lambda^n\leq L_n\leq C_L\lambda^n. \tag{27}
\]

## 6. Geometric bounds for the row sums

We transfer (27) to \(a_n\) using (17). Define
\[
C_a=\frac{a_{10}}{\lambda^{10}}+ rac{C_L}{\lambda-1}>0.
\]
Then \(C_L\leq C_a(\lambda-1)\). We prove inductively that
\[
a_n\leq C_a\lambda^n\qquad(n\geq10).
\]
The base case follows from the definition of \(C_a\). If it holds at \(n\), then by (17) and (27),
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{n+1}
&=a_n+L_n\\
&\leq C_a\lambda^n+C_L\lambda^n\\
&\leq C_a\lambda^n+C_a(\lambda-1)\lambda^n
 =C_a\lambda^{n+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]

For the lower bound, put
\[
c_a=\min\left\{\frac{a_{10}}{\lambda^{10}},
                   \frac{c_L}{\lambda-1}\right\}>0.
\]
Then \(c_a(\lambda-1)\leq c_L\). The base case gives
\(c_a\lambda^{10}\leq a_{10}\). If
\(c_a\lambda^n\leq a_n\), then
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{n+1}
&=a_n+L_n\\
&\geq c_a\lambda^n+c_L\lambda^n\\
&\geq c_a\lambda^n+c_a(\lambda-1)\lambda^n
 =c_a\lambda^{n+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence, for every \(n\geq10\),
\[
c_a\lambda^n\leq a_n\leq C_a\lambda^n. \tag{28}
\]

Taking positive real \(n\)-th roots in (28) yields
\[
c_a^{1/n}\lambda\leq a_n^{1/n}\leq C_a^{1/n}\lambda.
\]
For every fixed positive constant \(d\), one has \(d^{1/n}\to1\), for example by writing it as \(\exp((\log d)/n)\). Therefore both bounding sequences tend to \(\lambda\). By the squeeze theorem,
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \lim_{n\to\infty}a_n^{1/n}=\lambda},
\]
where \(\lambda\in(3/2,2)\) satisfies \(\lambda^4(\lambda-1)^3=1\). In particular, the conjectured limit exists.
